cards.q: What is the nominal yield strength of a class {ya}.{yb} bolt, in MPa?
cards.why: The first number × 100 is the tensile strength; the second, in tenths, is how much of it is yield.

cards.q: What tapping drill suits an M{d} coarse thread of pitch {p} mm, in mm?
cards.why: About diameter minus pitch.

cards.q: An M{d} bolt needs a preload of {f} kN, with a nut factor K = {kf}. Using $T = KFd$, what torque is that, in N·m?
cards.why: Preload in newtons, diameter in metres: $T = KFd$.

cards.q: A drawing is at a scale of 1:{s}. A line on it measures {m} mm. How long is the real part, in mm?
cards.why: 1:{s} means the real thing is {s} times bigger than the drawing. (Better still, use the dimension written on it.)

cards.q: On a sectional view, what does hatching show?
options: Hidden edges behind the surface
Solid material cut by the section plane
A knurled or deliberately rough surface
Parts that are bought in, not made
cards.why: Imagine the part sawn along the section line: hatching marks the sawn faces.

cards.q: A drawing uses first-angle projection (usual in the UK and Europe). Where is the plan (view from above) placed?
options: Below the front view
Above the front view
To the left of the front view
On a separate sheet
cards.why: First angle: each view is drawn on the far side of the one it looks from, so the view from above goes below. Third angle (US) puts it above. The title block shows which, with a symbol.

cards.q: A shaft is dimensioned Ø{d} ±{t} mm. What is the largest it may be, in mm?
cards.why: The upper limit is the size plus the tolerance.

cards.q: A Ø20 H7 hole is +0.021/0 mm, and a Ø20 g6 shaft is −0.007/−0.020 mm. What is the greatest clearance between them, in µm?
cards.why: Greatest clearance: the largest hole (20.021) minus the smallest shaft (19.980) = 0.041 mm = 41 µm. The least is 0 − (−7) = 7 µm.

cards.q: What kind of fit is H7/p6?
options: A clearance fit: a sliding fit
A transition fit
A loose running fit
An interference fit: a press fit
cards.why: Letters from p onwards on the shaft are above the hole's tolerance zone, so the shaft is always bigger than the hole.

cards.q: In a feature control frame, what are the letters A, B and C after the tolerance?
options: The inspector's initials
The required surface finishes
The datums it is measured from
Three alternative tolerances
cards.why: Datums are the reference features: the part is set up on A, then B, then C, and the feature is checked from them.

cards.q: A surface has a flatness tolerance of 0.05 mm. What does that mean?
options: The surface is exactly 0.05 mm thick
It lies between two parallel planes 0.05 mm apart
It is within 0.05 mm of datum A
Its roughness is no more than 0.05 µm
cards.why: Flatness is a form tolerance: it needs no datum, only two parallel planes enclosing the whole surface.

cards.q: A hole's centre is {dx} mm and {dy} mm (at right angles) from its true position. What diameter of position tolerance zone does it need, in mm?
cards.why: The offset is $\sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2}$ (Pythagoras); position zones are diameters, so double it.

cards.q: What does a fully constrained sketch mean in CAD?
options: Every size and position is fixed by constraints
The sketch is locked and cannot be edited
The sketch has been printed and signed off
The sketch has more than ten lines in it
cards.why: Then nothing can move by accident when you drag or change something, and design changes behave predictably.

cards.q: In an assembly, what do mates (assembly constraints) do?
options: Weld the parts together into one solid body
Set each part's material and its colour
Make the drawing sheet from the model
Locate parts, leaving only the intended movement
cards.why: Mates such as coincident, concentric and distance fix the parts' positions the way the real joints do.

cards.q: Put the usual CAD workflow in order.
cards.why: Sketches drive features; features make parts; parts make assemblies; drawings are made from the model, and follow it when it changes.

cards.q: A {m} kg block rests on a flat floor. The coefficient of friction is {mu}. What force does it take to slide it, in newtons?
cards.why: $F = \mu N$, and on the flat the normal force is the weight, mg.

cards.q: Why does it take more force to start something sliding than to keep it sliding?
options: The object gets lighter once it is moving
Air resistance helps once it is moving
Static friction is higher than sliding friction
Friction does not depend on movement at all
cards.why: Surfaces at rest settle into each other; once moving, the kinetic coefficient is lower. It is why slow axes can stick and then jump (stick-slip).

cards.q: A block sits on a ramp at {t}°. What is the smallest coefficient of friction that stops it sliding?
cards.why: Down-slope force $mg\sin\theta$ against friction $\mu mg\cos\theta$: it holds when $\mu \ge \tan\theta$.

cards.q: A {a}-tooth gear drives a {b}-tooth gear. The first turns at {n} rpm. How fast does the second turn, in rpm?
cards.why: Teeth pass at the same rate, so speed × teeth is the same for both gears.

cards.q: A {n} rpm motor has a {d1} mm pulley driving a {d2} mm pulley by belt. How fast does the driven pulley turn, in rpm?
cards.why: The belt's speed is the same at both pulleys: speed × diameter is constant.

cards.q: A gearbox has a {r}:1 reduction and is {e}% efficient. {t} N·m goes in. What comes out, in N·m?
cards.why: Torque rises by the ratio (as speed falls), less the losses.

cards.q: A ball screw has a {p} mm lead and turns at {n} rpm. How fast does the nut travel, in mm/s?
cards.why: Each revolution moves the nut one lead; rpm ÷ 60 is revolutions per second.

cards.q: A screw with a {p} mm lead and 90% efficiency is driven with {t} N·m. What thrust does it give, in newtons?
cards.why: Work in = work out over one turn: $2\pi T \eta = F \times lead$, so $F = \frac{2\pi T \eta}{lead}$, lead in metres.

cards.q: Why does a vertical axis on a ball screw usually need a brake?
options: Ball screws slip when they get warm
It is efficient enough for the load to back-drive it
The balls fall out when it is unpowered
The motor cannot hold at standstill
cards.why: Ball screws run at around 90% efficiency and are not self-locking: with the power off, a load on the nut back-drives the screw and the axis falls.

cards.q: Match each bearing with the load it suits best.
pairs: Radial load with some axial, at high speed
Combined radial and axial, usually in pairs
cards.why: Rollers carry more than balls; the contact angle decides how much axial load a bearing takes.

cards.q: A ball bearing's dynamic rating is C = {c} kN and it carries P = {p} kN. What is its L10 life, in millions of revolutions?
cards.why: For ball bearings $L_{10} = (\frac{C}{P})^3$ million revolutions (the power is 10/3 for rollers). Double the load: an eighth of the life.

cards.q: A ball bearing with C = {c} kN carries {p} kN at {n} rpm. What is its L10 life in hours?
cards.why: L10 in revolutions, then ÷ revolutions per hour (60 × rpm).

cards.q: Why fit a flexible coupling between a motor and a ball screw?
options: To take up small misalignment
To let the screw slip on overload
To make the axis run faster
To insulate the motor electrically
cards.why: A good servo coupling bends a little across its axis but stays stiff in twist, so it forgives misalignment without adding backlash.

cards.q: What happens if two linear rails under one carriage are not parallel?
options: Nothing: the blocks align themselves
The axis runs faster than before
Only the lubrication interval changes
The carriages bind and wear fast
cards.why: Rails have parallelism limits in microns; out of them, the blocks fight each other through the stroke.

cards.q: Aligning a coupling by the rim method, a dial gauge reads {a} mm at the top and {b} mm at the bottom. What is the offset between the shafts, in mm?
cards.why: The gauge swings round, so it sees twice the offset: half the total indicator reading.

cards.q: How much energy does it take to lift {m} kg by {h} m, in joules?
cards.why: Potential energy $E = mgh$.

cards.q: A hoist lifts {m} kg by {h} m in {t} s. What power does that take, in watts?
cards.why: Power is energy ÷ time: $\frac{mgh}{t}$.

cards.q: A hoist lifts {m} kg by {h} m in {t} s. The whole drive is {e}% efficient. What electrical power does it draw, in watts?
cards.why: Output power ÷ efficiency = input power. The difference turns to heat.

cards.q: A solid disc has a mass of {m} kg and a radius of {r} m. What is its moment of inertia, in kg·m²?
cards.why: Solid disc or cylinder: $J = \frac{1}{2}mr^2$.

cards.q: A shaft carries {t} N·m at {n} rpm. What power is that, in kW?
cards.why: $P = T\omega$, with ω in rad/s: rpm × 2π ÷ 60.

cards.q: A solid disc of {m} kg and radius {r} m is brought from rest to {n} rpm in {t} s. What torque does that take, ignoring friction, in N·m?
cards.why: $J = \frac{1}{2}mr^2$; $\alpha = \frac{\omega}{ t }$ with ω in rad/s; $T = J\alpha$.

cards.q: A fan runs at {n} rpm. What is its once-per-revolution (1×) vibration frequency, in Hz?
cards.why: Revolutions per second: rpm ÷ 60.

cards.q: A {m} kg mass sits on a spring of stiffness {k} N/m. What is its natural frequency, in Hz?
cards.why: $f_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{ k }{ m }}$: stiffer is higher, heavier is lower.

cards.q: A machine shakes badly at one speed in its range and is fine either side. What is likely, and a quick cure?
options: Imbalance: fit balance weights to the rotor at once
A loose bolt: tighten every fixing on the frame
Resonance: skip that speed band, then stiffen or retune
Bearing wear: change the bearings at both ends
cards.why: A peak at one speed is a natural frequency being excited. Most VFDs have skip frequencies; the lasting fix changes the stiffness or mass.

cards.q: Vibration is high at once per revolution, mostly radial. What is the likely cause?
options: Misalignment
Imbalance
A bearing defect
Electrical noise
cards.why: Imbalance is a once-per-rev force. Misalignment tends to show at twice running speed and in the axial direction; bearing faults at their own non-integer frequencies.

cards.q: A thermal image shows one phase terminal on a contactor much hotter than the other two. What is likely?
options: A poor connection on that phase
The motor is only lightly loaded
The contactor's coil is failing
Normal: one phase always runs hot
cards.why: Heat is I²R: a poor joint's extra resistance heats up under load. Re-make it (isolated) before it fails.

cards.q: An induction motor on 50 Hz runs at a slip of {s}. Broken rotor bars show sidebands at $f(1 \pm 2s)$. What is the lower sideband, in Hz?
cards.why: Motor current signature analysis: sidebands at 50(1 − 2s) and 50(1 + 2s) grow as bars crack.

cards.q: A tie carries {f} kN. Its cross-section is {a} mm². What is the stress in it, in MPa?
cards.why: Stress = force ÷ area; N/mm² is MPa.

cards.q: A {l} m bar stretches by {dl} mm. What is the strain, in microstrain (millionths)?
cards.why: Strain = extension ÷ original length, both in the same units; × 1 000 000 for microstrain.

cards.q: A steel bar (E = 200 GPa, or 200 000 N/mm²) {l} m long, {a} mm² in section, carries {f} kN. How much does it stretch, in mm?
cards.why: $\Delta L = \frac{FL}{AE}$, with every length in mm.

cards.q: A {l} m cantilever carries {w} kN at its free end. What is the bending moment at the wall, in kN·m?
cards.why: Moment = force × distance: the largest is at the wall.

cards.q: A simply supported beam of span {l} m carries {w} kN at mid-span. What is the largest bending moment, in kN·m?
cards.why: Each support takes half the load; at mid-span the moment is $\frac{W}{2} \times \frac{L}{2} = \frac{WL}{4}$.

cards.q: A simply supported steel beam (E = 200 GPa), span {l} m, second moment of area I = {i} m⁴, carries {w} N at mid-span. How much does it deflect, in mm? ($\delta = \frac{WL^3}{48EI}$)
cards.why: Everything in SI units (N, m, Pa), then × 1000 for mm. Deflection grows with the cube of the span.

cards.q: A shaft transmits {p} kW at {n} rpm. What torque does it carry, in N·m?
cards.why: $T = \frac{P}{\omega}$, with ω in rad/s. Slower shafts carry more torque for the same power.

cards.q: A solid shaft {d} mm in diameter carries {t} N·m. What is the largest shear stress, in MPa? ($\tau = \frac{16T}{\pi d^3}$)
cards.why: With T in N·mm (× 1000) and d in mm, the answer is in N/mm², which is MPa.

cards.q: How does a keyway affect a shaft?
options: It makes the shaft stiffer in torsion
It has no effect on the shaft's strength
It makes the shaft lighter and stronger
It concentrates stress and cuts fatigue strength
cards.why: Stress piles up at the keyway's corners; designs apply a stress concentration factor, and generous fillet radii help.

cards.q: What is fatigue failure?
options: Failure from a single large overload
Rust eating away at the metal
Cracking under repeated stress below yield
Bending once past the yield point
cards.why: Each cycle grows a small crack a little, until the rest breaks suddenly. The fracture face often shows beach marks.

cards.q: A part's material yields at {y} MPa. In service it sees {w} MPa. What is its factor of safety against yield?
cards.why: Factor of safety = strength ÷ working stress.

cards.q: What is a steel's endurance (fatigue) limit?
options: The highest stress it can take once
A stress below which it lasts indefinitely
The number of cycles before it rusts
The temperature at which it softens
cards.why: Many steels have one; aluminium alloys do not, so they are designed for a finite number of cycles.

cards.q: In design for assembly, what is asked of each part?
options: Does it need to be a separate part?
Can it be painted the same colour?
Is it from the cheapest supplier?
Is it heavy enough to be robust?
cards.why: A part earns its place only if it moves relative to others, must be a different material, or must come apart for service. Otherwise, combine it.

cards.q: A redesign removes {r} parts that each took {s} s to fit. At {v} assemblies a year, how many hours of assembly does it save a year?
cards.why: Seconds saved per assembly × assemblies ÷ 3600.

cards.q: Why not give every dimension a tight tolerance, to be safe?
options: Tight tolerances make parts weaker
Drawings cannot show tight tolerances
The standards forbid tight tolerances
Cost climbs: more operations, inspection, scrap
cards.why: Tolerance where the function needs it; leave the rest to the general tolerance.
